A Kind Unknown Elsewhere in the World—Much Whiter Than White Folks—Only One in Fifty of the Tribe is White—Their Curious Musical Instruments.
[BY RENE BACHEL]

One theory was that they were descendants of a lost Spanish colony of early days. In the valley of the Amazon there is a tribe, called Lorinzos, extremely naked and altogether envy, yet of very light complexion. It is a matter of historical records that, more than two centuries ago, they captured a fortified Spanish town by overcoming the defenders with clouds of smoke from anudge-tire lighted on the windward side, killed all the men, and carried off the women.
Among scientists there has been of late much discussion about those with Indians, but it may now be said that the problem has been fully settled.

Recent trouble with the Sun Thas Indians, of Panama, which has made necessary the sending of an American warship to keep the peace, causes greater interest by release of the fact that it is among those people that the white Indians, of my Stories origin, are found.
For the so-called white Indiums are not white folks at all. In our sense of the word. They are much whiter than we are having sling of a milky whiteness altogether different.

But there is no record of any such incident where the San dilas tribe is concerned, and no occasion for imagining that they have any Cuneusian blood.
After thorough study of the problem, the Smithsonian Institution has definitely decided that the white Indians of Panama are albinos. Their albinism, however, is of a wholly unfamiliar kind, for their eyes are blue, not pink, and their yellow hair has not the colourlessness of the ordinary human albino.

As will Ba remembered, eight members of the tribe were brought to Washington last October by Dr. R. O. Marsh, on his return from an exploring expedition in little-known regions of the Isthmus of Darien. In that expedition the Smithsonian Institution was represented. Five of the eight were of the ordinary copper colour; the remaining three were typical "white Indians."

So long ago as 1000, no explorer named Wefer wrote of them: "There is one complexion so singular among a sort of people in this country that I never saw or heard of the like of them, in any part of the world. They are white, of both sexes. Their skins are not such a white as those of fair people among Europeans, but milk white, lighter than the colour of any European, and much like that of a white horse. For there is this further remarkable in them, that their bodies are beset all over with a fine, short, milk-white down, which adds to the whiteness of their skins. They are not a distinct race by themselves, but now and then one is bred of a copper-coloured father and mother."

This description could not now be improved upon. Among the San's Blue people, it is not unusual for parents of normal Indian colouring to have children with skins of a peculiar milky whiteness, blue eyes and yellow hair. In some institutions the white skin is disfigured by blotches of light brown. A married couple may have both dark and white children. Or light brown parents may produce white and dark brown offspring.
Curiosities of Heredity.

The tribe does not regard with favour this freak of albinism, and is disposed to segregate white children of both sexes at the age of puberty. Hence there is a tendency to intermarriage among white individuals, whose descendants after two or three generations of such matings are all of them milk-white. Thereby works out in familiar law of heredity, such as govors, with white rats, white mice, and white rabbits. Albinism is one of nature's favourite freaks, and she ready perpetuates it.

The San Blas Indians inhabit a long stretch, about 120 miles of the Caribbean coast of Panama, the territory they call their own including the San Blas range of mountains, which parallels the seashore, from five to twenty miles back. They call themselves Tulo, and say that their ancestors dwelt around the base of Tarsecuna Mountain, west of the mouth of the Atrafo River, the highest peak in that region. It was there that the great god Olokkuppil created the tribe.

They are friendly folk, with an advanced social organization, and a principal chief who is in effect a king. Up to the present time they have kept aloo from the whites as far as possible, knowing that contact with them would inevitably work their doom. The recent trouble down there was due to an attempt to annex their domain to Colombia, which, being determined to maintain their independence, they resisted. Bloodshed resulted.

Their families occupy separate houses, with wall-built community houses for meetings and tribal ceremonies. They are good farmers, raising rice, bananas, sugar-cane, chocolate and coffee, also a long-steple cotton, which they dye and weave into cotton cloth and hammocks. They are expert fishermen, diving into deep pools and catching fish with their hands.

The men wear breecheloths and the women skirts, in both cases supplemented by a tunic. The cotton tunics are decorated with applique designs in a material of contrasting colour. The women wear nose rings and earrings and bracelets of silver; also armlets and anklets which, being
The San Blas Indians are industrious workers. A man's wealth depends on the success of his efforts to push back the jungle and keep it back, enabling him to plant and grow crops for food and fruits to sell. In tropical regions nature is hostile to agriculture, because weeds and wild plants generally grow so fast that unceasing labour is required to keep them down. It is for that reason that civilization have always had their beginnings in desart countries, such as Arabia and Egypt.

The principal social event is a wedding, to which people come from all the neighbouring villages. They dance and sing for several days, adorning themselves with wreaths of gry flowers. The celebration continues for as many days as the father of the bride, who pays for the entertainment, can afford.

The language of that tribe of Panama exceeds in softness and beauty the malicious Castilian. A vocabulary of over 8,000 words has been assembled, and while the eight San Blas Indians were in Washington, dictaphone records of extended discourses were made, to serve for further study of the tongue.
Songs With Stories.

One of those Indians was a chief named Igwa Nigidppi, who had made a special study of the songs of his tribe. He is a man of intelligence and artistic culture; and, expecting to succeed before long the very aged king, is acquiring a knowledge of the geography of the region, with its irregular coast line and hundreds of islands and "keys". He drew for the Smithsonian scientists a map showing the location of villages, with the approximate number of inhabitants in each.

Chief Nigdlppi and one of his followers interested the scientists very much be rendition of tribal songs with stories, of which diotaphone records were made. One of them told the story of a race between dugout canoe with sails. A storm broke, followed by a calm and a favouring breeze, the song ending with an account of the wedding of the winner, at which rivals in the contest danced.

There is no musical accompaniment these sons. Nevertheless, the San People do not lack musical instrument which are of various kinds entirely strata to us. One of them is a shell trumpet. Others are bone whistles, flutes, Pops, and gourd rattles. The trumpet is a conch shell, its tip, pierced with a hot to which the lips are applied. Whilst are made from the wing-bones of polka: sing buzzards.

The flute is a reed of another kind much larger, with two fingersholes. It is made by pushing out the pith with the stiff quill of a wild turkey's tail, the holes being thereupon burned through with hot iron and shaped with a sharp knife. The player shakes a gourd rattle with his right hand while fingering the flute with his left.

The Pan-pipes, made of reeds, are sometimes two or three feet long, and are capable of emitting surprisingly loud and resonant tones, resembling the hoots of steam calliope. They are used to accompany dancing and for serenading young women. A web consists of two parts, played by two players. One player sounds a note, and the other the next note, alternately, the melody being improvised.
Rattles For The Babies.

The gourd rattle, commonly used to accompany dancing, contains pebbles, and is pierced by a stick which serves as handle. Another kind of rattle is for putting babies to sleep. Inside of it are number of small pebbles and one large one. When shaken, there is a rattling of the small pebbles, with a rolling murmur of the big one, which continued, has peculiarly soothing effect.

MICA, A FREAK AMONG MINERALS
MICAMINE SOUTH DAKOTA
This Remarkable Product Finds Use in Many Lines of Industry—Insulating Qualities Make It Vital To Electrical Equipment.
一
[BY FRANKLIN JOHNSON.]

Commonplace though it be, nice, is an unreal that will bear looking into. It is a product with a history and a future. Just how far it dates back into the story of mankind has never been discovered. The best we can do for it is to concede that its utilization was pre-historic—that the substance was known and used before the days of written records.

MICA MINE,
NEW HAMPSHIRE

Evidence of this has been placed before me in the mics mines of western North Carolina. In these places the miners regard it as in no wise uncommon to find buried evidence of the use of mics by the Indians who occupied that part of the country before the days of Christopher Columbus. The evidence is in the form of mute testimony from the aboriginals, afforded by discovery of stones implements left in the mines by the people who delved there before the advent of the white man. These implements are unearthed in trenches, pits and mounds of present day operations. Their relation to any distinct period of time is altogether unknown, and can be touched in no other way but by a process of approximation and dedication. They may, even, have anated the American Indians. The hammers and axes unearhed in these diggings are some times of a typo totally unlike those of the Red Man; and there is ample ground for the inference that the mining of mics was practised by a race to which the Indians were more juniors.
Modern Industry Is Comparatively New.
Mica-mining in the modern sense is of comparatively recent development. The real activity in the mines of North Carolina came after the close of the Civil War. It was not until 1807 that the demands of industry gave rise to activities working of the rich deposits of this remarkable mineral. Since then the users to which the product is applied have expanded in generous, ratio. Today's employment is widespread and important.

One of the great consumers of mica is the electrical industry. In this line of manufacture, the mineral is one of the essential materials. The product is brought into play wherever non-inflammable insulation is required. It is used in sheets, in wathers and in disks. In the machinery of oldก็ dynamos the substance is indolomable. The same status exists as to electric light cockets, spark plugs, guards in rhinoclasts and the overpreschillable boxes. In every telephone mouthpiece and receiver it is essential to the translation and delivery of the

humm.voice. Without this mineral there would be a severe handicap or the conversation of the busy business man using the telephone to save himself an arduous journey, and that of the modern flapper who spends Dad's money in long distance petting parties, regardless of expense.
This condition holds good throughout the additional output. In apparatus and fixtures there is widespread use of flexible cloth and tape covered with mica for purposes of installation. In the photograph that turns on the jazz the mineral is an important part of the diaphragm. In the equipment of radio the same importance is found. In short, the scientist would be forced to do some brisk thinking in providing a substitute if the world's supply of mica were suddenly eliminated.

Most of the uses so far mentioned pertain to the mineral in the form of sheets. This is just the beginning. Ground mica has a place of no less importance. In this form the substance plays a part in many industries. The sparkling particles on the wallpaper of your room are more than likely tiny fakes of this particular agent of civilization. In the manufacture of the roof palms the product is a vital commodity. It is used in the manufacture of rubber goods, boiler, coverings and insulating compounds; in patent roofing materials, in mouldings, and in the process of printing the widely used cloth known as calloo. How Mined.

The men's belt of North Carolina furnishes more than half of the mica total production of the United States. The mineral occurs in bodies of rock that the geologists are pleased to term pegmatite or highly metamorphic formations. I am willing to confess that the geologists had something on me when they made this statement. Not until they told me some of the common names of the rocks did I gather what they were trying to tell me. With the information thus translated, I learned the "the rocks are garnet, stauro-lite, hornblends, and granite" gnisses. Much of the production comes from small out-croppings, which are worked in simple fashion, by farmers, or by miners and prospectors conducting operations on a small scale. In activities of this kind, workers are apt to be intermittent. When crops or other duties demand attention the production of mica is temporarily suspended. A number of large mines have been developed on good-sized scale, and the output of these more ambitious operations has done much to stabilize the production and the condition of the market.
